title: Heads, dependents, complements and adjuncts
summary: From zero: what a phrase and its head are, how to find the head, the difference between required and optional dependents (arguments vs adjuncts, complements vs adjuncts) with the four tests, how to draw a dependency diagram, and head directionality in English, Japanese and Arabic.
sourceNote: Week 4 handout (Heads and dependents), Essentials of Linguistics ch. 6.2 to 6.3, Tallerman ch. 4.1 to 4.2. Rebuilt for readers who missed class: phrase, head, argument, complement and adjunct are each defined before they are used.

sections.heading: Start here: phrases and their heads

blocks.body: A group of words that works as **one unit** in a sentence (a constituent, from the universals chapter). *Several large books* is a phrase: you can replace all three words with *they*.

The **one word** in a phrase that decides what kind of phrase it is and what it's about. Every phrase has exactly one head. The other words in the phrase are its **dependents**: they add detail to the head.

blocks.md: **One example.** *Several large books* is about **books**. *Several* and *large* just add detail (how many, what size). So *books* is the head, and *several* and *large* are its dependents. Here is the easiest way to find a head: drop words one at a time. The one you can't lose is the head.

blocks.caption: The drop test. Losing 'several' or 'large' leaves a books-phrase. Losing 'books' leaves nothing to be about. Hover each row.

blocks.body: A phrase is named after the category of its head. Head is a noun → **NP** (noun phrase). Verb → **VP**. Preposition → **PP**. Adjective → **AdjP**. Adverb → **AdvP**. So *several large books* is an NP, and *with a loud thud* is a PP because its head is the preposition *with*.

columns: Why that word is the head
rows: it's about books; the rest describes them
a preposition heads its phrase and needs the NP after it
it's a request; *for privacy* says what kind
it's a kind of proud; the rest says how and of whom
blocks.title: Handout (1): find the head, name the phrase

blocks.body: A head **selects** its dependents: it decides what kind of words may go with it. A noun takes an adjective (*the loud yawn*, '*the loudly yawn'), a verb takes an adverb (*yawned loudly*, '*yawned loud'). Some heads even pick an exact word: you're fond **of** something, never '*fond with'.

blocks.md: **Heads can pick meaning too.** *The speaker informed the audience* is fine, but *#The earthquake informed the audience* is odd: *inform* wants someone who can mean to tell you something. That's why it gets `#` (grammatical, but strange), not `*`.

blocks.prompt: What is the head of *the old man from Ohio*, and what kind of phrase is it?
blocks.answer: **man** (a noun), so it's an **NP**. Drop *man* and you have *the old from Ohio*, which isn't about anything.

blocks.prompt: What is the head of *right under the bed*?
blocks.answer: **under** (a preposition), so it's a **PP**. *right* and *the bed* depend on it.

blocks.md: **Where you'll meet this** Search engines reduce your query to its head before matching: 'cheap flights to Osaka' is about *flights*. Dependency parsers (spaCy, Stanza) output exactly the head-to-dependent links from this chapter, and apps read 'who did what to whom' straight off them.
blocks.label: world

sections.heading: Required or optional: arguments and adjuncts

blocks.body: A dependent that is **required** by the verb's meaning: the participants the action can't happen without. *Savor* needs someone savoring and something savored, so both are arguments. (This is valency from Week 2: yawn 1, savor 2, give 3.)
A dependent that is **optional**: extra detail about how, when, where, why. You can always drop it and the sentence stays grammatical. *loudly*, *yesterday*, *in the garden*.

lines: [The bear] yawned [loudly].
frames.caption: Handout (6). Try deleting each bracket. What you can drop is optional; what you can't is required.

lines: [The bear] yawned [loudly].
The bear yawned.  ✓   → 'loudly' is optional: an ADJUNCT
frames.caption: Drop 'loudly': still a fine sentence. So 'loudly' is an adjunct.

lines: [The bear] yawned [loudly].
The bear yawned.  ✓   → 'loudly' is optional: an ADJUNCT
*Yawned loudly.  ✗   → 'the bear' is required: an ARGUMENT
frames.caption: Drop 'the bear': broken. The yawner is required, so 'the bear' is an argument.

lines: [The bear] savored [the berries] [slowly].
*The bear savored slowly.  ✗   → 'the berries' is an ARGUMENT
The bear savored the berries.  ✓   → 'slowly' is an ADJUNCT
frames.caption: Next verb: 'savor' needs something savored. Drop 'the berries' and it breaks; drop 'slowly' and it's fine.

lines: [The bear] gave [me] [a huge fright] [last weekend].
arguments: the bear, me, a huge fright   (3: ditransitive)
adjunct:   last weekend
frames.caption: Three arguments (the giver, the one who got it, the thing given) and one adjunct (when). The count of arguments is the verb's valency from Week 2.

blocks.md: **The one-line version:** ==what you can drop is an adjunct; what you can't drop is an argument==. Always test by deleting, then say what happened.

blocks.prompt: *She put the keys on the table after lunch.* Which dependents of *put* are arguments?
blocks.answer: *she*, *the keys*, and *on the table* (*She put the keys* is incomplete). *after lunch* is an adjunct: drop it and nothing breaks.

sections.heading: Complements vs adjuncts: the four tests

blocks.body: A dependent that the head **picks out** and keeps **right next to it**. drafted **a screenplay**, fond **of music**, into **the house**. Most complements are required. Complement is the word syntax uses for the head's chosen partner; argument is the word for a required participant.

**The one exception:** the subject is an **argument** (it's required) but **not a complement** (it sits on the other side of the verb and isn't the verb's chosen partner). *The bear* in *The bear savored the berries* is an argument, not a complement. The trees in Week 6 show why.

rows: How many can a head take?
A limited number, usually 1–2, fixed by the head
Potentially unlimited (yawned loudly, yesterday, in the garden, for an hour…)
Need not be adjacent; freer order
Yes: category and often the exact preposition ('resort TO', 'fond OF')
No: attaches to almost any head of that type

rows.label: Where?
rows.right: can move: In the garden, he sang

rows.label: Picked by the head?
rows.left: yes, even the exact word: resort TO

blocks.title: Six phrases
blocks.body:
For each, what is the complement and its category?

1. **into** [the house]: complement NP. A preposition always takes exactly one NP complement.
2. **drafted** [a new screenplay]: complement NP. Drop it: *'She drafted' is odd; 'draft' selects an object.
3. **set** [the packages] [on that shelf]: TWO complements, NP and PP. 'Set' requires both: *'set the packages' is incomplete.
4. **wondered** [whether she left]: complement is a clause (CP) introduced by the complementizer 'whether'. 'Wonder' selects a question-clause.
5. **resorted** [to his back-up plan]: complement PP, and 'resort' selects specifically 'to' (*'resorted with'). Selection of the exact preposition = complement.
6. **fond** [of classical music]: complement PP of the adjective. 'Fond' requires 'of' (*'fond' alone is odd as a predicate: *'She is fond').
blocks.slide: Handout (11): complements of the bolded heads

blocks.title: Sorting both
blocks.body:
For each bolded head, which dependents are complements and which adjuncts?

1. quietly **serenaded** his beloved in the garden with a guitar: complement: NP 'his beloved' (obligatory, adjacent, selected). Adjuncts: AdvP 'quietly', PP 'in the garden', PP 'with a guitar': all droppable, stackable, movable ('In the garden, he quietly serenaded his beloved').
2. repeatedly **glanced** at the clock nervously before noon: complement: PP 'at the clock' (glance selects 'at'). Adjuncts: 'repeatedly', 'nervously', 'before noon'.
3. unbelievably wealthy **relatives** of mine: complement: PP 'of mine' (the noun 'relative' wants a possessor). Adjunct: AdjP 'unbelievably wealthy'.
4. extremely **proud** of each student: complement: PP 'of each student' (proud selects 'of'). Adjunct: 'extremely'.
blocks.answer: Complements hug the head and are limited; adjuncts stack and float.

blocks.md: **Position, the handout's question.** In English, complements come **right after** the head: serenaded **his beloved**. Adjuncts can come before or after, outside the complement: **quietly** serenaded his beloved **in the garden**. ==Complements hug the head; adjuncts stack and float.==

blocks.prompt: *She glanced at the clock nervously.* Complement or adjunct: *at the clock*? *nervously*?
blocks.answer: *at the clock* = complement (glance picks *at*; it sits right after the verb). *nervously* = adjunct (droppable, movable: *Nervously, she glanced at the clock*).

sections.heading: Dependency diagrams: heads drawn as arrows

blocks.body: A picture of a sentence where an **arrow goes from each head to each of its dependents**. Every word has exactly one arrow coming in, except one: the **root**, which is the main verb (the head of the whole sentence).

blocks.md: **One example.** In *The bear yawned*, draw *yawned → bear* (bear depends on yawned) and *bear → The* (the depends on bear). *yawned* has no arrow coming in, so it's the root.

lines: Several large books fell to the ground with a loud thud.
fell → books        (the subject depends on the verb)
fell → to           (PP 'to the ground' depends on the verb)
fell → with         (PP 'with a loud thud' depends on the verb)
books → several, books → large
to → ground,  ground → the
with → thud,  thud → a,  thud → loud

Notice where the verb's arrows land: on 'to' and 'with': the heads of their phrases: never on 'ground' or 'thud' directly. If your homework diagram has an arrow landing inside a phrase from outside, you've skipped a head. Hover any word cluster.

blocks.body: An arrow from outside a phrase must land on that phrase's **head**. The verb's arrow goes to *to* in *to the ground*, never straight to *ground*. If an arrow lands in the middle of a phrase, you skipped a head.

blocks.prompt: Handout (7a): 'a huge fright'. Draw the arrows.
blocks.answer: fright → a; fright → huge. Head: fright (N). Two dependents, both adjuncts/modifiers of the noun.

blocks.prompt: Handout (7c): 'in the middle of the night'.
blocks.answer: in → middle; middle → the; middle → of; of → night; night → the. Head of the whole phrase: 'in' (it's a PP). 'of the night' is a PP complement of the noun 'middle'.

blocks.prompt: Handout (10): 'The brown bear slowly savored a huge dinner of very round red berries.' What is the root and what are its direct dependents?
blocks.answer: Root: savored. Dependents of savored: bear (subject; bear → the, brown), slowly (adjunct), dinner (complement; dinner → a, huge, of; of → berries; berries → round (→ very), red).

sections.heading: Head directionality: head first or head last?

blocks.body: The order of head and complement. **Head-initial**: head before complement (English, Spanish, Tagalog, Arabic). **Head-final**: head after complement (Japanese, Hindi/Urdu, Turkish). SVO is one head-initial pattern (V before its object); SOV is head-final. Subjects are not complements, so they don't count.

blocks.md: **One example.** English says ate **an apple** (head *ate* first). Japanese says *ringo-o tabe-ta*, 'apple ate' (head last). Same meaning, mirrored order.

blocks.caption: Handout (13)–(15) as mirror images. Green boxes are heads; the blue arrow always runs head → complement. English aims every arrow rightward (head-initial); Japanese aims every arrow leftward (head-final): verb, adposition, and noun all flip together. That all-at-once consistency is what makes directionality a parameter rather than three coincidences. Hover any row.

blocks.md: The point for the oral exam: directionality is *consistent* within a language. Japanese puts every head last: verb after object, postposition after noun, noun after its PP. English and Arabic put every head first. ##Once you know a language's setting from one pair, you can predict the others.## That's what 'parameter' means.

blocks.prompt: Korean is SOV with postpositions (handout Week 1: 'bang-eseo', room-in). Predict: does the noun come before or after its PP complement?
blocks.answer: After. Korean is head-final throughout, so 'picture of a robot' will be [robot-of] picture, like Japanese.

sections.heading: If this is your oral-exam concept

blocks.md:
- Definition: phrases are built from one head plus dependents; the head fixes the category and core meaning.
- Why it matters: it explains why 'several large books' acts like a noun, and why heads restrict what they combine with (*the loudly yawn).
- Two kinds of dependent: complements (selected, limited, adjacent, usually obligatory) vs adjuncts (optional, unlimited, movable). Give 'fond of music' vs 'quietly serenaded … in the garden'.
- The one exception to remember: subjects are arguments but not complements.
- Cross-linguistic hook: head directionality: English/Arabic head-initial, Japanese head-final, with one glossed pair each.
- Live problem: 'Take this sentence, find the head of each phrase, and sort the dependents': narrate each test as you apply it.

rows: A group of words that works as one unit.
The one word that decides what a phrase is and is about.
Any other word in the phrase; it adds detail to the head.
Phrases named after the category of their head.
A head choosing what may go with it (fond OF, not fond WITH).
A required participant of the verb.
An optional add-on: how, when, where, why.
The head's chosen partner, right next to it; usually required.
The word with no arrow coming in: the main verb.
Head before its complement (English, Arabic) / after (Japanese).
blocks.title: Words from this chapter

exercises.title: Complement or adjunct? Run the diagnostics
exercises.prompt: 'She put the keys on the table yesterday.' Find the head of the VP and sort *the keys*, *on the table*, and *yesterday* into complements and adjuncts using at least two of the four diagnostics each (obligatoriness, ordering, iteration, 'do so' replacement).
hints: Start with obligatoriness: which phrases can you delete and still have a grammatical sentence? Delete one at a time.
The trap is 'on the table': it's a PP, and PPs are 'usually adjuncts'. But try deleting it: '✱She put the keys.' Some verbs *require* a location. Obligatory → complement, whatever its category.

'Do so' replaces the verb plus its complements. 'She put the keys on the table yesterday and he did so today' ✓: 'today' is outside 'do so', so 'yesterday' is an adjunct. Try '✱…and he did so on the floor': it fails, so 'on the table' is inside.
solution: *the keys*: obligatory ('✱She put on the table'), can't be iterated, inside 'do so' → complement.
*on the table*: obligatory with *put* ('✱She put the keys'), can't be replaced by another location after 'do so' → complement. A PP complement: category doesn't decide.
*yesterday*: optional, can be stacked with other time adjuncts ('yesterday, after lunch'), outside 'do so' ('…and he did so today' ✓), freely reordered → adjunct.
So: put [the keys] [on the table]: two complements: plus the adjunct [yesterday].
exercises.why: Complements are what a verb *requires*; dictionaries call this valency and NLP calls it a subcategorization frame. Every dependency parser, every verb-sense lexicon, and every 'this sentence is missing something' grammar error depends on getting exactly this distinction right.

exercises.title: Draw the dependency diagram
exercises.prompt: Draw the dependency diagram (head → dependent arrows) for 'The old professor from Kyoto gave a very long lecture on syntax.' Name the root and list every head with its dependents.
hints: Find the main verb first: that's the root. Then ask of every other word: which word does it depend on? An adjective depends on its noun; a determiner on its noun; a PP's preposition depends on whatever it modifies; the preposition's NP depends on the preposition.

Two frequent errors: hanging 'from Kyoto' on the verb instead of on 'professor' (who is from Kyoto? the professor: so it modifies the noun), and making 'very' depend on 'lecture' instead of on 'long'.
Each word has exactly one head, except the root. Count your arrows: n words → n − 1 arrows.
solution: professor → The, professor → old, professor → from; from → Kyoto.
lecture → a, lecture → long, lecture → on; long → very; on → syntax.
exercises.why: Dependency diagrams are the format of Universal Dependencies, the treebank standard used by spaCy, Stanza, and most modern parsers. If you ever look at parsed output in a corpus, this is what you'll be reading.

exercises.title: Find the head
exercises.prompt: What is the head of *a very tall glass of water*?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
solution: **glass.** Drop it and *a very tall of water* makes no sense.
exercises.why: Finding the head is the first step of every tree and every dependency diagram.

choices.feedback: Yes: it's a glass; 'of water' says of what.
Water is inside the PP 'of water', which depends on glass.
Of heads the smaller PP 'of water', not the whole phrase.

exercises.title: Argument or adjunct?
exercises.prompt: *He fixed the sink yesterday.* What is *yesterday*?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
solution: **Adjunct.** It's optional and could go on almost any verb.
exercises.why: The deletion test settles most of these in one step.

choices.feedback: Yes: drop it and 'He fixed the sink' is fine.
It isn't required: the fixing happens with or without it.
It isn't picked by 'fixed'; any verb can take 'yesterday'.
The head of the VP is 'fixed'.

exercises.title: The subject exception
exercises.prompt: In *The dog chased the cat*, is *the dog* a complement of *chased*?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
solution: **No.** *The dog* is an argument (required) but not a complement; *the cat* is the complement.
exercises.why: The handout flags this as the one place the two words split.

choices.text: No: it's an argument, but not a complement
choices.feedback: Right. Required (argument) but not the verb's chosen partner on its right.
Required makes it an argument, not automatically a complement.
You can't drop it, so it isn't an adjunct.

choices.text: Yes: it's next to the verb
choices.feedback: Being next to the verb isn't enough; the complement is 'the cat'.

exercises.title: Head-initial or head-final?
exercises.prompt: Turkish says *ev-de* 'house-in' and *elma yedim* 'apple I-ate'. What is its setting?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
exercises.why: Once one pair tells you the setting, you can predict the others: that's what makes it a parameter.

choices.feedback: Yes: the postposition and the verb both come after their complements.
Both pairs point the same way.
Two pairs agree, which is enough to predict the rest.
